baslik: Hackers Backdoor Nextcloud Servers Through Critical Flaw in Collabora’s Built-in CODE App
govde:
Attackers exploited a flaw in an optional Nextcloud app, Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server, to plant web shells on Nextcloud servers. Three administrators reported the issue on GitHub, with the first logged attack on September 10.

A web shell is a small file that executes any command an attacker sends via a web request, with the rights of the web server account. The flaw allows an unauthenticated request to run a command on the server, but only when the app's local document server is not running, such as during a restart or upgrade, or after a crash.

Collabora fixed it in version 26.4.303 on September 11 and on October 14 published an advisory with the identifier CVE-2026-110447, warning that turning off the app does not help: it must be updated or removed.

The app, published by Collabora under the package name richdocumentscode, downloads a copy of Collabora Online Development Edition (CODE) and runs it on the Nextcloud server itself.

That lets Nextcloud Office edit documents without a separate Collabora server. Its store listing says it is "for local testing and non-production use" and "for personal use or for small teams."

Collabora's advisory covers every version before 26.4.303 and says standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected. A warning posted on the Nextcloud community forum on October 3 stated that an installation is not affected if it uses only the Nextcloud Office app ( richdocuments) without the built-in app, whether its Collabora server runs in Docker, from a Linux package, or at a hosting provider.

The app's proxy.php script starts the local CODE server whenever a request arrives, and nothing is listening. In versions up to 26.4.302, the script placed text from the request, including its path, inside a double-quoted bash command, where the shell still runs anything written as $(...).

baslik: curl Patches HTTP/2 Upload Flaw After PoC Demonstrates Client-Side Code Execution
govde:
A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine.

The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash instead.

The flaw, a use-after-free tracked as CVE-2026-92392, affects curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, both the command-line tool and the library that many other programs use for transfers. curl rates it High on its own four-level scale, its first High-severity flaw since the SOCKS5 heap overflow of October 2023. The project cut its release cycle by two weeks to ship the fix.

The attack runs from the server side. The client has to upload a file of roughly 135KB over HTTP/2 to a server controlled by the attacker, and the server's certificate must pass the client's checks. libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for https:// URLs when the server offers it, and the library was built with HTTP/2 support.

The flaw has shipped in every curl release since 8.12.0 in February 2025. No source reports attacks that use it. The reporter's HackerOne write-up, with the malicious server script and a Docker container described as reproducing the code execution, became public on October 14 with the advisory.

What to Install, and What to Do Until Then

Upgrade to 8.23.0 or apply the fix commit to a local build. curl's machine-readable advisory also lists fixed versions on three older branches, and the project said it would ship updated Rock-solid curl releases, its long-term-support line for customers with support contracts, in step with 8.23.0:

8.20.x branch: 8.20.2

baslik: How to Run a Deepfake Readiness Drill Before a Cloned Voice Calls Your Team
govde:
Cloned voices and synthetic video calls now show up in payment fraud, help desk resets, and access requests. A structured drill shows security teams exactly where verification breaks down, while nothing is at stake.

The call comes in at 4:40 on a Friday. It's the CFO, or it sounds exactly like her, asking the controller to push a supplier payment out before the weekend because a deal closes Monday. She's traveling, she's rushed, and she apologizes for the bad connection. Ten minutes later an email lands with the wire details.

A couple of years ago that scenario was a conference talk. Now it shows up in incident reports. In a 2025 Gartner survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, 62% said their organization had experienced at least one deepfake attack in the prior 12 months. In the same survey, 43% reported at least one deepfake audio call incident and 37% had run into deepfakes on video calls.

And the wire is only the obvious ask. The same cloned voice can call the help desk to move an MFA token, or ask an identity admin to set up a new global admin ahead of an "audit." A fraudulent wire tends to surface at reconciliation. A quietly added admin account can sit there for months.

Most organizations have a policy that says to verify unusual payment and access requests. Far fewer have checked whether that policy survives a phone call from someone who sounds like the person who signs off on everyone's paycheck. A deepfake readiness drill is how you find out, on your own schedule, with nothing real on the line.

Why detection by ear falls short

Security awareness training has long taught employees to look for tells. Awkward phrasing, an odd sender address, a link that doesn't match the text. Voice clones and real-time face swaps leave fewer of those tells every quarter. Asking people to hear the fake is asking a lot.

baslik: Researchers Used a Public OpenAI Model to Build a $250,000 Chrome Full-Chain Exploit in Six Days
govde:
A team at security firm XBOW chained three then-unknown Google Chrome bugs into a single attack that runs code on a Windows computer when the user only loads a web page, the company said.

Its researchers built the attack in six days by directing AI agents running OpenAI's publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model. Google has since confirmed all three bugs, fixed them, and paid XBOW its top $250,000 reward for a full Chrome exploit.

The attack is a full chain: a set of bugs used together to break every layer of Chrome's protection, from a web page all the way to the computer.

Chrome runs web page code inside two nested sandboxes, the barriers that stop a hacked page from reaching the rest of the machine. The chain crossed both. The result was code running outside Chrome on Windows, with no need for the user to click or download anything.

All three bugs are now fixed, and XBOW says they were never used against Chrome users. The two that carry public identifiers were fixed in Chrome 152.0.7977.65 on August 25 and 152.0.7977.82 on September 3.

Chrome updates on its own, but the fix only takes effect after the browser restarts, so the action is to relaunch Chrome and confirm the version is 152.0.7977.82 or later.

The six days are the headline, and they need their frame. XBOW built the awarded chain between Sunday, August 2, and Friday, August 7, during the Black Hat and DEF CON conferences in Las Vegas. That sprint followed months of earlier work: the company set the challenge at a January staff meeting in Malta, and its first full Chrome chain took two months to complete.

One version of the awarded chain nearly failed when a bug it relied on turned out to be one Google already knew about. XBOW had built the exploit in swappable parts with backups ready, so it replaced that part and the chain held. By the company's own count of its usage logs, the six-day run cost about $40,000 in AI charges.

baslik: An AI Agent Found a Critical OTP Bypass in Production. The Attack Was the Easy Part.
govde:
The bug was simple: the login let you choose where your sign-in code went. Proving it on a live website was the hard part.

During an authorized assessment, an AI pentesting agent found a critical authentication bypass on a major insurer's production website, on its own.

One login request let the user choose where the one-time passcode went.

The attack was the easy part. Proving it on a live site took web context built over a decade.

The Login Worked. Then the Agent Stopped.

Reflectiz's AI pentesting agent was mapping the login flow of a major insurer's production website, which has millions of users.

The agent requested a login code and directed it to an email inbox it controlled. The code arrived. The login went through. Its guardrails halted the test after the login succeeded.

The agent had discovered a critical-severity authentication bypass on its own. Reflectiz reported it to the insurer.

The Flaw: The Request Chose Where the Code Went

A one-time passcode (OTP) only proves who you are if it goes somewhere already linked to the account. Here, that link was broken.

The login request carried two fields that decided delivery: the channel and the address. Normally, the code went by text to the phone number on the account. But the request could change the channel. Switch it to email, and the server sent the code to whatever address the request named, not the address registered to the account.

Simplified, the request looked like this:

The server never checked that the address belonged to the account.

Binding a code to its account is one of the most basic checks in authentication. OWASP's testing guide asks this in plain words: "Are the OTPs tied to the correct user account...?"

An attacker with the required customer identifiers could potentially use the flaw to access that customer's account.

baslik: AI-Found Linux Kernel Flaw Gives Local Users Root, and Can Break a Guest Out to the Host
govde:
A flaw in Linux's vhost subsystem lets a local user read and write kernel memory at will and become root across nearly a decade of kernel versions. In one virtualization setup, it lets an untrusted virtual machine write to the host's memory and hijack the program that runs the virtual machine.

The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-74580 and named Vghost. Tencent Zhuque Lab, which found the flaw, released a fix on August 3 and published a full write-up on October 12 with working demos of both attacks. There is no public sign it has been exploited yet.

vhost is the part of the Linux kernel that speeds up network and other input/output for virtual machines and containers. A local user reaches it by opening a device node, usually /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock.

On the host, the flaw gives an unprivileged user a reliable way to read and write any kernel address, bypass KASLR, and escalate to root. The attack is deterministic: it needs no memory grooming and no lucky timing.

The second attack is narrower. When a virtual machine's virtio device is placed behind a virtual IOMMU with iommu_platform turned on, and vhost runs in device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can trigger the same bug and make the host kernel write out of bounds into the host's QEMU process. From there, a guest can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and take control of where the host process runs next, or crash it.

vhost keeps a small cache of the memory mappings behind each virtual ring and the shared queues it uses to move data. A cache hit is treated as proof that the region was already checked. The cache is cleared when the mapping is updated or invalidated and when the queue is reset, but not when the VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR or VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM commands change the ring's addresses or size while the queue is live.

baslik: UK Legal Aid Agency: Hackers stole records dating back to 1978
govde:
The Legal Aid Agency (LAA), an executive agency of the UK's Ministry of Justice that manages the country's Public Defender Service, says attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating back to 1978.

The agency employs around 1,250 staff, oversees billions in legal funding, and works with approximately 2,000 providers, including barristers, solicitor firms, and non-profit organizations that deliver civil and criminal legal aid services in England and Wales.

The LAA disclosed the cyberattack in early May 2025, warning that payment information for legal aid providers might have been compromised.

Two weeks later, it confirmed the resulting data breach was more serious than first believed after finding that attackers had stolen a large trove of sensitive applicant and recipient data from 2010 onward, including contact details, dates of birth, national ID numbers, criminal history, employment status, as well as contribution amounts, debts, and payments.

The threat actors have also stolen legal aid providers' data, including provider contracts, office locations, financial information, contact details, LAA Online Portal credentials (including names and email addresses), and more.

In an update published this week, the LAA said follow-up analysis of the exfiltrated data found that the stolen records go back almost five decades.

"The vast majority of the LAA data relates to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and 16 May 2025, or to cases that were live during this period. However, we have now confirmed that approximately 250,000 records predate 2007," the agency said. "The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978."

Customers running older, unsupported versions must upgrade to a supported release.

Palo Alto says there are no known workarounds for the vulnerability, but customers with Threat Prevention subscriptions can enable signatures that provide limited protection against known attack patterns.

"Limited coverage in Threat Prevention means that while known attack patterns can be identified using the current Threat ID, variations may exist that cannot currently be detected," warns Palo Alto.

"If this CVE and Required Configuration for Exposure impact your environment, we recommend upgrading to an unaffected version."

The vulnerability was discovered internally by Suraj Siddharudh, a senior principal product security researcher at Palo Alto Networks.

Famous Chollima (a.k.a. WageMole) is commonly tracked as a North Korean threat actor associated with fraudulent IT-worker schemes that generate revenue for the DPRK regime.

CrowdStrike researchers say that DPRK IT workers used several methods to send the company-issued laptops to the "farm," instead of the address in the provided identity documents:

Submit fake theft reports to trigger replacement shipments to the farm’s address

Rotate through residential addresses to obscure the final destination

Claim last-minute relocations to divert devices mid-shipment

Abuse IT staffing roles they sometimes hold to covertly redirect shipments

The Always On VPN remote access solution replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and works with domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server devices.

govde:
By Sila Ozeren Hacioglu, Security Research Engineer at Picus Security.

For years, security teams had a window of several weeks between a CVE going public and attackers exploiting it. Every year, that window got smaller. Then Mythos-class models arrived, and attackers can now weaponize a new CVE within hours. That leaves security teams very little time to find out whether they’re exposed.

That’s where offensive testing comes in. But it has traditionally run on a schedule. Over the years, that schedule got tighter. Annual pentests became quarterly, and automated penetration testing tools made weekly testing possible.

Each advancement shortened the time a change could go untested. Traditional automated pentesting worked fine back when exploitation took weeks. Now that attackers have made a big jump, offensive testing is making one too.

That jump is agentic pentesting. It’s the sharp edge of offensive testing today, but it has blind spots. This piece looks at where they are and how to close them.

How Agentic Pentesting Should Work

A manual pentest usually goes through several phases: reconnaissance, vulnerability assessment, initial access, post-exploitation, and reporting. Traditional automated pentesting tools follow the same phases. Even before LLMs took off, some advanced tools used machine learning to choose the next step. For example, five years ago, we built our Attack Path Validation (APV) product with such a decision engine. But AI agents take it further.

In agentic pentesting, one or more AI agents carry out a pentest step by step. In our agentic pentesting product, Picus Swarm uses five specialist agents orchestrated by Numi AI.

AI pentest agents evaluate findings and your organization’s context to choose the next step dynamically. That creativity lets them find exploit chains much faster than a human pentester, including some a human might miss entirely. However, creativity comes at a cost.

govde:

Researchers identified malicious copies of eight banking apps that use a hooking engine to bypass app-signature, Accessibility, and Play Integrity checks by substituting certificate information or returning empty lists.

ThreatFabric found that the malicious copy of a banking app retains almost all of the original app’s code, but loads a hooking engine built on the open-source frameworks YAHFA and Dobby.

When launched, the patched app performs the following evasion actions:

Substitute the genuine signing certificate when queried.

Hide enabled Accessibility services.

Remove screenshot protection, allowing remote viewing and recording.

Volexity Uncovers Stealthy Ivanti VPN Attack Using Three Zero-Day Vulnerabilities

Ivanti VPN zero-days let attackers gain root access, steal credentials, evade detection, and prepare for wider network compromise.

On October 5, Volexity started investigating suspicious activity at one of its monitoring customers and traced everything back to an Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliance running version 22.8R2.4, the latest build available at the time. Three chained zero-days gave an unknown attacker unauthenticated root access.

“n the first week of October 2026, Volexity discovered an unknown threat actor, UTA0576, abusing a zero-day exploit chain to compromise a fully patched (at the time, version 22.8R2.4) Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliance.” states Volexity. “This exploit chain combined an authentication bypass, a remote code execution (RCE), and a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution. The RCE and authentication bypass vulnerabilities are tracked under CVE-2026-104935.”

The attacker, tracked as UTA0576, had been inside the device since at least October 3, two days before anyone noticed. Ivanti released a patch for two of the three vulnerabilities on October 13; the privilege escalation fix is still coming in a future release.

The first flaw affects welcome.cgi, the public login page. An attacker sends a request to this page that passes the authentication checks but includes the path to a protected internal script in an HTTP header. The system checks the URL to decide whether to allow the request, but uses the header to decide where to send it. This mismatch allows the attacker to bypass authentication.

The attacker then uploads a Perl script disguised as a ZIP file through another endpoint. The server saves the file, checks whether it is a valid ZIP archive, and schedules it for deletion when the check fails. Before the file is deleted, the attacker sends multiple requests to its predictable location on disk

baslik: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th)
govde:
Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary]

[This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Crypto mining malware has been active and spreading across the internet for quite some time now. Moreover, the DShield honeypot picked up a worm that self-propagates through a plethora of means. One of them is stealing SSH keys after it gains access to a system. Furthermore, it also leverages a rootkit to maintain access to infected systems. One would hope that threat actors would have moved on past this worm by now. However, due to its rudimentary design and its effectiveness, they have had no reason to move on.

A malicious binary was uploaded and executed on the DShield honeypot, and that is where a copy of the Panchan worm was obtained. It is written with Golang, and it is a peer-to-peer botnet. Moreover, this worm was first identified in 2022. Many vendors recognize this worm now as seen below.

Therefore, a system with security controls such as egress filtering, ingress filtering, access control lists, continuous monitoring, and passwordless authentication will prevent this worm from taking root. However, many systems are insecure and unpatched. This is why this worm is still propagating across the internet. The strings captured from the binary below show how simple it is to find its command-and-control channel and the functions that it consists of.

Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system

baslik: TAG-193’s Regional Espionage Operations
govde:
TAG-193’s Regional Espionage Operations

Government Targeting across the Region

TAG-193’s targeting extends across government institutions responsible for diplomacy, economic development, agriculture, and environmental management. These organizations hold information that can inform negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions. Across Central Asia, shared river systems and interconnected energy and transport infrastructure give such information particular strategic value.

Our research examined TAG-193 campaigns from early 2025 through May 2026, identifying activity involving government entities in Russia, Tajikistan, Belarus, Armenia, and Uzbekistan. Lure documents and impersonated services indicated additional targeting interests across the region. Together, these findings suggest a sustained intelligence-collection mission encompassing diplomatic priorities and the management of natural resources.

Diplomacy, Water Security, and Resource Management

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. Additionally, activity involving a Belarusian agriculture-related government entity preceded a senior bilateral meeting in Astana. While these temporal associations do not establish that the TAG-193-related activity was connected to the described developments or reveal what information the operators sought, they do provide context indicating TAG-193’s targeting interests.

TAG-193’s recurring interest in environmental and resource-management institutions is also noteworthy. Observed activity involved an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and infrastructure associated with Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initia

baslik: Microsoft drops an actively exploited zero-day among record high of 1,413 vulnerabilities
govde:
Microsoft drops an actively exploited zero-day among record high of 1,413 vulnerabilities

Microsoft’s streak of record-breaking vulnerability disclosures continued with a mega Patch Tuesday, containing 1,413 defects affecting the company’s various enterprise products and services.

The monthly batch of patches surpassed the company’s previous annual record of 1,261 common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) set in 2020.

“Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception — now it’s the baseline,” Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, wrote in an email. AI is partly to blame, he added, but it “isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.”

Yet, for defenders understandably overwhelmed by the surge of defects found in Microsoft products, actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities aren’t growing in kind.

“If there’s solace to be had, it’s in the fact that only one of these bugs is under active attack,” Childs wrote in a blog post. “If you go back to the hot 0-day summer of 2023, there were 17 Microsoft 0-days between January and October as opposed to 15 this year during the same period.”

Microsoft disclosed one actively exploited zero-day affecting Windows Shell — CVE-2026-96951 — that allows unauthorized attackers to bypass a security feature. The high-severity defect is the third Windows Shell vulnerability exploited this year, according to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable.

“There have been 26 Windows Shell vulnerabilities patched in 2026 through October, a staggering figure compared to previous years, with only 3 Windows Shell CVEs in 2025 and just one in 2024 and 2022,” he added.

Members of Congress are pressing the Trump administration to expand the federal government’s role in securing artificial intelligence, wanting new safety standards and regulations, independent testing of models and more “aggressive” use of AI for defensive cybersecurity purposes.

“These incidents come as AI systems are becoming dramatically more capable at discovering software vulnerabilities, writing and executing code, using digital tools, and operating autonomously,” the senators wrote.

Microsoft collaborated with Japanese authorities, Health-ISAC and several cybersecurity companies to dismantle an expansive, seemingly disconnected ecosystem of Chinese-language cybercrime tools and services, the company announced Wednesday.

More than three-quarters of those malicious messages targeted Microsoft customers, the company said.

Cybercriminals purchased the phishing kits, tools and infrastructure from an interconnected network Microsoft and Japanese authorities started investigating in early 2025. The kits were used to target individuals and organizations in healthcare, financial services, logistics and IT predominantly in the United States and Japan.

Microsoft said it and Health-ISAC, working with a federal court order, seized and redirected domains that powered the underlying infrastructure of these cybercrime tools and services known as YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man.

baslik: Flock CEO: We haven’t ‘fired’ any police departments as customers
govde:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said that his company has not ended any contracts with its customers over abuse of its products.

Speaking to TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos at the Disrupt 2026 conference in San Francisco, Langley responded to criticisms facing the company about the misuse of its license plate reader cameras by police departments. It comes after streams of reporting identifying dozens of police officers who have been arrested, fired, or told to resign after being caught abusing access to Flock’s nationwide database of license plate detections, oftentimes to stalk people without permission.

Langley told Loizos that the company would end a relationship with a customer where there was clear widespread abuse of its systems. “If a customer knowingly broke the law, we would fire them immediately. That’s very easy,” Langley said.

“Most of the debate is nuanced into ‘what if two officers out of fifty were caught?’ Today, we haven’t fired any customers, but it’s not off the table in the case of some pretty drastic law-abiding issue,” added Langley.

The abuse of Flock’s systems and the data it collects is the latest in an array of controversies embroiling the Atlanta, Georgia-based maker of license plate reader cameras. Flock has more than 100,000 cameras around the United States, which allow local police departments and federal agencies to track the whereabouts of vehicle license plates and people as they pass by.

By allowing its law enforcement customers to track license plates outside of their jurisdictions, some police departments can track cars across the entire country through Flock’s national central database.

baslik: Apate sends AI agents undercover to get scammed so they can gather fraud intelligence
govde:
Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or to speed up workflows. Apate.ai sends them undercover to get scammed.

Founded in 2024 on the basis of research done in Macquarie University in Sydney, the Australian startup deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, sporting different ages, genders, and accents, and speak various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

The company says its fleet of agents has so far wasted 17 years of scammers’ time across 2.5 million conversations. More importantly for Apate’s customer base of banks, telecom companies, government agencies, and utilities, the undercover agents try to get scammers to reveal things about themselves that are usually learned only after a victim has been scammed: bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites, the brands they’re impersonating, and other details about the scams they’re running.

Apate, one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, then feeds that information to its customers, who use it to inform their anti-fraud measures and initiatives. (The company will pitch a panel of VC judges at Disrupt, which is taking place this week at Moscone West in San Francisco through Thursday, October 15.)

It’s a curious evolution of scam-baiting, but it’s not so surprising given how much AI has empowered scammers and hackers. baslik: As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
govde:
The Yam Store sold kits that helped criminals impersonate organizations, steal credentials, and target more than 75,000 organizations worldwide; AI-assisted analysis helped identify the infrastructure behind the operation.

Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages.

Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS).

The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials.

Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities.

“Working together, and with the assistance of AI tools, we connected accounts, websites, and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them,” Steven Masada, associate general counsel and GM for Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post. “What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.”

The evolving PhaaS marketplace

An attacker could exploit the bug by planting a malicious file in a public repository and waiting for a developer to ask Claude Code to inspect it, Noma said in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Wednesday.

Once the application rendered the file, the script could read local files and exfiltrate sensitive data, including AWS credentials, GitHub secrets and SSH private keys, to a remote server.

Attackers without an account of their own were found logging in to Ivanti Connect Secure appliances using an authentication bypass flaw that the vendor has since fixed. Once inside, attackers ran arbitrary commands on the appliances.

“Ivanti initially discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of our product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0,“ the vendor said in a security advisory. ”We had been working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions when exploitation occurred.”

According to security firm watchTowr’s vulnerability FAQ, the flaw allowed remote attackers to spoof the signals used to establish a user’s identity, bypassing normal authentication checks. The bypass uses a path separate from normal authentication, so existing login protections do not stop it, watchTowr added.

Tracked as CVE-2026-104935 and rated at CVSS 8.6 out of 10, the vulnerability affects multiple product branches, including Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 and earlier, as well as specified 25.1 releases. Ivanti says versions 22.7 and earlier are not affected.

Ivanti has released fixes, including for versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1, depending on the hardware and software branch. Security teams were advised to identify their deployed versions, apply corresponding fixes, and investigate potential compromise.

While Ivanti said reliable indicators of compromise were not yet available, Volexity, the cybersecurity firm credited with discovering the flaw, has published details of its exploitation. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the flaw to its known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 13.

baslik: Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
govde:
We keep buying better security tech, but the real gaps are ownership and follow-through, so cybersecurity can’t stay the CISO’s problem alone.

When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015, the environment looked very different.

Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon.

Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller.

Much has changed since then.

But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question:

Why are we still discussing so many of them?

Technology has advanced enormously. Investment has increased. Regulation has expanded. Cybersecurity has achieved unprecedented executive and board visibility.

Yet organisations still struggle with governance, accountability, organisational silos, short-termism and execution.

Those were management problems in 2015. They remain management problems today.

The ‘what’ was never the hardest part

One of the central observations behind my early work was that the what of cybersecurity was already reasonably well understood.

Standards, control frameworks and good practices had existed for years. Organisations could identify weaknesses, define controls and produce remediation plans. They knew what good cybersecurity looked like.

The difficult questions were always the how and the who.

govde:

In this Help Net Security interview, Michael Scott, CISO at Immuta, talks about how organizations should handle permissions for AI agents. He argues agents should be treated as lower-trust identities that don’t inherit everything their user can access.

Scott explains why agent privilege creep differs from the human kind, how authority should pass to sub-agents, and why authentication alone does not secure what an agent does. He predicts at least two major enterprises outside the AI sector will suffer a critical AI-related incident within 18 months.

The first thing I want to know about an agent is what identity it operates under, and whether that identity is dedicated to the agent or based on the user’s permissions.

It is not uncommon for an agent to have excessive permissions, especially when the agent is using the user’s credentials, which can vary across users. Agents may leverage access to other resources not intentionally targeted by the human user, like available APIs, as an example.

I think we need to start treating agents as lower-trust identities. They’re not human, so they don’t necessarily approach a task the way a human would. They can find ways to accomplish something that nobody anticipated when the permissions were originally granted.

I’d want to know what the agent can access and why, and whether those permissions disappear when the work is finished. An agent shouldn’t retain broad access simply because it might need it again someday.

I see it as a different problem. With employees, privilege creep usually happens gradually. Someone moves into a new role or gets access for a temporary project, and those permissions stick around long after they’re needed. It’s a problem security teams know how to identify, even if they’re not always great at fixing it.

Elsewhere in its scans, the internet-scanning company measured much slower movement. Exposed industrial control systems rose about 4% in two and a half years. baslik: FBI raids 40+ laptop farms helping North Korea pocket US tech salaries
govde:
FBI raids 40+ laptop farms helping North Korea pocket US tech salaries

North Korean IT workers used stolen and fabricated identities to land remote jobs at more than 70 US companies, with help from Americans who allegedly kept company-issued laptops running from their homes, according to the US Department of Justice.

Arrests in Ohio, raids in Texas

Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas were taken into custody under an Ohio indictment for wire fraud, money laundering and identity theft. The same indictment names ten China-based defendants, and the identities of two more remain under seal.

Prosecutors allege that from 2019 to about July 2025, the two men and their co-conspirators received devices issued by the victim companies, installed remote-access software on them and sent the earnings, about $3 million, to accounts controlled by North Korea.

The victims include health care, communications, retail and manufacturing companies in 17 states and the District of Columbia.

In Texas, FBI agents searched more than 40 suspected “laptop farms” between September 21 and 25 as part of Operation Lonestar Roundup, seizing about 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices.

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas.

“It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability.” Raybould noted.

US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI disrupt the operation, tracks this group of North Korean IT workers and their helpers as “Famous Chollima.”

People who have shopped with Phase Eight, Hobbs or Whistles will have to wait to find out whether their personal information was exposed in a cyberattack on the company behind the three UK fashion brands.

TFG London, the UK business of South African retail group The Foschini Group (TFG), detected the incident on Sunday, 11 October 2026.

In a statement released on Tuesday, the company said the attack hit some of its IT systems, specifically those used by Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles. Inside Story and White Stuff, two other brands in the same business, were not affected.

After detecting the incident, TFG London activated its incident response and business continuity plans and brought in outside cybersecurity specialists to contain the attack. It has also reported the incident to the relevant UK authorities.

“TFG London’s stores remain open and trading, although several of its IT systems remain unavailable. The Group’s operations in TFG Africa and TFG Australia run on separate systems and are not affected,” the company said.

The statement does not say what kind of attack took place or how the attackers got in, and at the time of writting it is unknown who is behind the attack.

“The investigation is ongoing, including establishing whether any personal or other sensitive information has been compromised,” the company added.

If the investigation finds that such information was compromised, TFG London said it will notify the people and organizations affected.

The TFG London incident is the second attack on a UK retailer disclosed in a week. Days earlier, fashion retailer ASOS was the victim of a cyberattack, which customers found out about after the hackers sent push notifications to users of the company’s mobile app.

North Macedonian police arrest alleged administrator behind OLVX cybercrime market

The administrator behind a cybercriminal marketplace called OLVX was arrested this week in North Macedonia in a joint operation between the Balkan country’s Ministry of Interior and the FBI.

The suspect was not named, but the FBI and North Macedonia said a raid on the man’s home in the village of Golema Rečica was conducted after charges were filed.

Since 2023, OLVX has become a popular market where cybercriminals share stolen personal data, login credentials and other tools to help with cybercrime.

“Active between 2023 and 2025, OLVX is alleged to have unlawfully sold victims’ personally identifiable information and login credentials via over 1,500 seller accounts,” the FBI said in a statement. “The existence of this marketplace directly endangered the digital security of thousands of American citizens who rely on the integrity of accounts they use.”

North Macedonian police said the suspect also ran another group called ONEMILI on Telegram that offered tools for fraudulent refund schemes and other scams.

“Additionally, evidence was obtained indicating that the suspect had acquired and possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) for personal use through the Telegram application,” North Macedonia’s Interior Ministry said.

Cybersecurity firm ZeroFox published a lengthy investigation into OLVX in 2023, warning that the site was becoming increasingly popular among cybercriminals selling phishing kits, remote desktop connections, credentials, stolen data and other tools.

The site allowed criminals to pay each other through cryptocurrency instead of operating an escrow service like many other underground marketplaces. Users loaded funds onto the site and paid each other with the funds sent to the platform.

The investigation began three years ago when a large number of Russian-speaking victims in Brooklyn told prosecutors they responded to Facebook ads in Russian offering investment opportunities. When the victims tried to take their money out, they were locked out of their accounts and told they had to pay additional fees and taxes in order to get their funds.

Gonzalez’s office said victims likely lost millions but authorities were able to claw back about $300,000 worth of stolen funds.

Several of the seized websites were made to look like legitimate investment platforms and referenced U.S. government agencies or wealthy people like Elon Musk.

The servers contained victim information, data for the websites and operational software. The seized data also showed that the scammers were running a secondary operation where they would contact victims weeks after the initial scam and offer to recover their stolen cryptocurrency for a price.

Polish investigators said they found evidence showing a spyware manufacturer harvested data from Polish opposition leaders and other victims and transmitted it to Israel.

govde:
Microsoft takes down 3 major phishing platforms used by Chinese cybercriminals

Microsoft on Wednesday announced legal action disrupting three powerful phishing platforms used by Chinese cybercriminals to send hundreds of millions of malicious messages impersonating over 75,000 organizations worldwide.

The tech giant worked with Japan’s National Police Agency and healthcare cybersecurity organization Health-ISAC to obtain a U.S. court order seizing and redirecting domains that were part of the infrastructure underlying YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man.

Since January, the three platforms collectively enabled more than 750 million messages targeting Microsoft customers alone.

These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators. The goal of most of the tools is to steal credentials, personal information, banking data and other login information.

Iron Man is a phishing-kit-as-a-service operation that offers cybercriminals more than 2,300 pre-built lure pages impersonating trusted services like postal companies, traffic fine offices, tax agencies, banks, telecoms and more. Iron Man’s customers purchase a subscription that offers thousands of templates tailored for Australia, Japan, India and dozens of other countries.

CoGUI provides criminals with ready-made websites and messages that can impersonate trusted brands, companies, government agencies and financial institutions.

CoGUI was used heavily to target people in Japan but cybercriminals began shifting to Iron Man by the middle of 2026. In addition to the templates allowing criminals to impersonate brands, Iron Man allowed thieves to “quickly deploy email, text and web content tailored to specific brands, industries and countries.”

govde:
Russian travel booking platform suspends reservations after cyberattack

Russian online travel agency Anywayanyday has temporarily suspended new bookings after a cyberattack on its IT infrastructure, leaving customers unable to purchase airline and train tickets or book hotels through its platform, the company said on Wednesday.

The agency's website remains unavailable as it works to restore its systems. Previously confirmed reservations remain valid, Anywayanyday said, without providing a timeline for resuming normal operations.

“We have already taken steps to strengthen our security and are working to restore service availability,” Anywayanyday said in a statement, adding that it had found no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.

The company did not identify the attackers or disclose how its systems were breached.

Launched in 2008, Anywayanyday is one of Russia's oldest online travel booking services. As of 2025, the platform had partnerships with approximately 800 airlines and 330,000 hotels.

The cyberattack comes as Russia's aviation industry faces widespread disruptions following a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks targeting Moscow.

More than 500 flights have been delayed or canceled at airports serving the Russian capital since Tuesday evening, while Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, has imposed temporary restrictions on arrivals and departures at all four major Moscow airports.

Russian airline booking systems have previously been targeted by hackers. In 2023, a large-scale distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack disrupted the Leonardo airline reservation system, affecting several Russian carriers and causing flight delays at airports.

The files recovered from the exposed infrastructure suggest preparation for post-compromise operations and potential activity against Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.

Unit 42 Uncovers PEERSTITCH, a Stealthy FortiGate Implant

By:Daniel GottShawn Westfall

Tags:ApacheCL-STA-0954LoggingNetwork intrusionNetwork SnifferPayloadReverse shellsVPN

Unit 42 investigated a multi-stage network intrusion against a telecommunications organization that occurred in September 2024, which we are tracking as cluster CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820). The attackers behind CL-STA-0954 achieved an initial compromise by exploiting CVE-2024-47575 against a centralized FortiManager appliance.

From that single appliance, our observations are that the attackers exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Those firewalls protected the target's own infrastructure and the networks of its clients.

Following the initial compromise, the attackers behind CL-STA-0954 demonstrated a complex level of tradecraft. Aspects of the post-exploitation activity overlap with intrusions attributed to suspected nation-state actors. Armed with the stolen information, the attackers:

Maintained long-term access

Intercepted network traffic

Established VPN sessions

Exploited a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability

The attackers exploited another vulnerability, CVE-2025-61624, via FortiOS auto-script path traversal. This exploit facilitated the deployment of PEERSTITCH, a novel, memory-resident ARM64 malware.

PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections. Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection.

The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network.

## The Future of AI Cryptanalysis

Matthew Green [has](https://x.com/matthew_d_green/status/2107992246360649879)[been](https://x.com/matthew_d_green/status/2108278850555674975?s=46)[writing](https://x.com/matthew_d_green/status/2108552414978564418) a rather pessimistic series of posts about the potential for AI systems to vastly outperform humans in cryptanalysis of both symmetric and public-key ciphers.

I am more optimistic than he is. That is, I have stronger faith in the over-engineering cryptographers tend to do. I am trying to write this up in more detail.

baslik: Cyberattack on Connected Fridges in France
govde:
Cyberattack on Connected Fridges in France

Another IoT cyberattack, this one in France:

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

Any IoT device that can’t be updated is vulnerable. And, probably, any IoT device that can be updated is also vulnerable.

baslik: China-Linked Hackers Exploited BeyondTrust Zero-Day to Take Over Remote Support Servers
govde:
The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance.

"The vulnerability exists within internal components of Remote Support," BeyondTrust said in a Thursday alert. "The components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages it received. Under the right conditions, this could be used to perform file operations on the appliance."

Patches for the flaw have been pushed to all Remote Support SaaS customers as of October 9, 2026. Self-hosted customers of Remote Support running versions from 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 are advised to manually update to BT26-05-RS patch. Customers running a version older than 24.3.1 will be required to upgrade to a newer version to apply the fix.

According to a timeline of events shared by BeyondTrust, Armory Castle is said to have exploited the flaw as a zero-day on a single self-hosted Remote Support appliance on August 29, 2026. Then, on September 27, 2026, "successful exploitation of another security device provider [became] public," it added, prompting it to initiate an investigation to hunt for similar activity.

baslik: CERT-In Warns AI Agents Accessed Sensitive Data at Indian Organizations During Testing
govde:
AI agents being tested online reached the live systems of Indian organizations and read business records, including personal data and confidential material, CERT-In said in an advisory on October 15.

The agents went beyond their assigned tasks, and none of the organizations detected the unauthorized access. After internal reviews, the AI companies whose models were being tested voluntarily reported the cases to CERT-In, India's national cyber agency.

AI agents are software systems that can plan work, run commands, use tools, and act on the internet autonomously for extended periods. In these cases, the agents gained access via credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configuration and public code repositories, and via cloud service roles with excessive permissions.

CERT-In did not name the AI companies, their models, or the organizations and sectors involved. It did not say how many companies reported cases or how many organizations were affected, and said only that the reports came in recently.

It also did not say whether any data the agents read was copied or kept, or whether the affected organizations have been told.

Attackers Used Open-Source AI Agent Tools in a Separate Campaign

CERT-In's own threat hunting found a second, separate set of incidents: a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. The attackers misused publicly available offensive-security frameworks built on AI agents.

The frameworks continue to be misused and rebranded, with numerous deployments across infrastructure in several countries. CERT-In did not name the frameworks or the attackers.

In this campaign, the frameworks cut the time from first access to final impact from days to a few hours, according to CERT-In. The attackers ran several agents in parallel for hours to days to reach their goals. Victims that only partly fixed the problems were attacked again within days, at a larger scale.

baslik: PEERSTITCH Malware Deployed via FortiOS Flaw Bypasses Checks on Tagged VPN Sessions
govde:
A suspected advanced threat actor has been observed exploiting a security flaw in Fortinet FortiOS to deliver a previously unreported memory-resident ARM64 malware known as PEERSTITCH.

The attack involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS score: 5.4), a path traversal flaw in the command line interpreter of FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager that could allow a privileged attacker to achieve arbitrary write or delete files via specifically crafted arguments to existing commands. "PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers Daniel Gott and Shawn Westfall said. The cybersecurity company said it discovered the activity as part of its prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider that took place in September 2024. baslik: Critical PwnEscape Linux Kernel Vulnerability Lets Guest VMs Read Host Memory
govde:
A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it.

The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape, is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart.

It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack.

What the Researcher Showed

Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets.

The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it.

Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment."

baslik: Citizen Lab Traces Zero-Click Candiru Spyware Infections at Al Jazeera to Targeted Online Ads
govde:
Candiru, an Israeli maker of spyware sold to governments, infected devices at the news network Al Jazeera through ordinary online ads, in attacks that needed no click or other action from the user, researchers at the Citizen Lab said Thursday.

The hidden attack code ran the moment an ad loaded on the screen, and in some cases the ad loaded out of sight, in the background.

The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, said this is the first public, technical confirmation that mercenary spyware, meaning hacking tools sold to governments, has reached real devices through targeted ads. The method had been described before from leaked company documents, but not shown in a live attack.

The researchers recovered the spyware itself from one device, but not the exploit that breaks into the browser or app to install it. That first break-in step is described from how the attack was set up, not from captured code.

How the Attack Worked

The ads were placed by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a normal digital advertising firm. Each ad carried a small piece of code that, when the ad loaded, quietly sent the device's advertising ID and internet address back to a Discover-Tech server, the researchers found.

That server decided whether the device belonged to a target. If it did, the server sent back attack code for the browser or app to run. If it did not, the server sent nothing. Because the ad itself carried no attack code, the ad networks that delivered it had nothing harmful to detect.

At Al Jazeera, at least 45 devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, the Citizen Lab said, and it linked the attacks to Candiru with high confidence. The researchers did not say which government was behind the operation.

govde:

The activity, observed from June 2025 through August 2026, involves four different infection chains that make use of macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and crafted WinRAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088.

baslik: NGINX Fixes 5 Flaws, Including Possible RCE and a TLS Bug That May Skip Client-Cert Checks
govde:
NGINX released versions 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 on October 14 to fix five vulnerabilities, one of them present in every release since May 2005.

There are three memory bugs that F5, the company behind NGINX, says could crash a worker process or possibly let an attacker run code, and each requires a specific configuration to exploit.

A fourth lets an attacker forge a TLS session that could get past client-certificate checks, though F5 calls the forgery non-deterministic and beyond the attacker's control. The fifth lets an HTTP/3 client slip extra bytes into a request that NGINX passes on to a backend.

None of the five was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 15, and neither NGINX nor F5 reports attacks. NGINX rates all five medium. F5 scores the three memory bugs 9.2, Critical, on CVSS v4.0, the TLS flaw 8.3, and the HTTP/3 flaw 6.9.

Which Configurations Are Exposed

Every one of the five needs a directive you added: an alias with a rewrite, a regex map, AIO with SSI, a shared TLS session cache, or HTTP/3. NGINX's own documentation recommends the shared session cache and request buffering; the other condition for the HTTP/3 flaw is on by default.

The TLS flaw sits in the automatic rotation of session ticket keys. Session tickets let a client resume a TLS session without a full handshake, and since version 1.23.2, from October 2022, a shared session cache makes NGINX generate and rotate the ticket keys itself unless you load keys from a file.

Each worker process keeps a copy of three key slots. Rotation copied only two, so the third slot held whatever was in memory before, and a ticket naming that slot could be verified and decrypted with that uninitialized key material, "allowing a forged session," the fix commit says.

One code-execution flaw is in React Server Components, and the other in librsvg, the open-source library Next.js uses through the sharp package to handle SVG images.

govde:
Drupal core has a critical flaw in its Field UI module that could let an attacker run code on the site's server, and fixes were shipped on October 14 in Drupal 11.4.10, 11.3.19, and 10.6.19.

An attacker cannot reach the flaw through core alone, the Drupal Security Team said in its advisory. Several exploit paths exist through contributed modules, and at least one known path needs no login.

Tracked as CVE-2026-108097, the flaw sits in Field UI, the core module behind the admin pages where site builders manage fields and how they display. Drupal rates it 19 out of 25 on its own risk scale, the level the project calls critical.

The advisory does not name the contributed modules that open a path to the flaw, and custom code may also expose it. Drew Webber of the Security Team and Octavio Galland are credited with reporting it.

Drupal 12.0.0 beta: 12.0.0-beta2, which is not for production use

No fix: Drupal 11.2.x and below, 10.5.x and below, and Drupal 8 and 9, all of which are end-of-life

Both 11.3.x and 10.6.x lose security coverage in December 2026.

In the week starting October 4, 151,442 of the 531,499 sites that reported their Drupal core version to drupal.org (28.5%) were on a branch that the advisory lists as affected and that received no fix.

A site that cannot update yet can uninstall the Field UI module, field_ui, which "will provide protection while sites are updated," the advisory says. The admin pages for managing fields and their display are unavailable while the module is uninstalled.

Field UI is installed by Drupal's Standard install profile, so a site built from that profile has the module unless someone removed it.

baslik: Why AI Confidence Is Not Validation
govde:
AI is already part of digital forensics and incident response work, with or without a policy in place to govern it. The issue is that these tools are growing more confident in their own output faster than practitioners are developing reliable ways to verify it. Without governance models and validation standards in place, that gap compounds and rarely stays contained to a workstation: an unverified finding can end up in a forensic report, a deposition, or in court.

At SANS, we created two new AI frameworks this year to help address this challenge: the Digital Forensics & AI Investigations Framework, which we mapped to the trusted standards established by the Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence (SWGDE), and the Incident Response & AI Investigations Framework, which we mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Both frameworks rest on the same principle: AI can accelerate investigative work, but the human examiner remains the final authority at every phase.

Where Validation Cannot Be Delegated

In digital forensics, validating an AI finding starts at the source file. A tool that doesn't show its reasoning has already produced an unreliable result, regardless of the confidence score attached to it. A tool that cites the specific file it parsed — for example, a claim that browser history came from Chrome's own database — gives an examiner somewhere to start. The claim is plausible at face value, but it still has to be confirmed independently before anyone treats it as fact.

I think of a high-confidence AI output the way I'd think of a third grader insisting the homework is finished. Saying it's done isn't the same as it being done correctly, and no amount of confidence changes that. The only way to know is to verify it, the way a parent checks the homework instead of taking their child's word for it alone.

baslik: Langflow's Critical Authenticated RCE Flaw Targeted in 1,423 Honeypot Exploit Attempts
govde:
Threat actors are exploiting a critical security flaw in Langflow, according to an alert from Previdian.

Langflow is an open-source platform that allows developers to build artificial intelligence (AI) applications and agentic workflows. In February 2025, DataStax, the parent company of Langflow, was acquired by IBM.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-105740 (CVSS score: 9.9), a case of authenticated remote code execution impacting versions prior to 1.9.0.

"Any authenticated Langflow user can achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server by adding an MCP server with the 'stdio' transport," reads an advisory released last month.

"The user-supplied command field is passed directly to bash -c "exec {command}" with zero validation, no allowlisting, and no sandboxing. The crux of the vulnerability is that Langflow accepts a user-provided command without restricting it to approved executables. This, in turn, can lead to shell execution.

In a hypothetical attack scenario, a bad actor can exploit the flaw in the following fashion -

Login as a regular, non-admin user.

Add a malicious MCP server by sending a crafted HTTP POST request to "/api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}" with a command field containing a malicious payload (e.g., a reverse shell).

The server accepts and stores the attacker-supplied "command" without any validation.

Trigger the flaw by fetching the MCP server list via an HTTP GET "/api/v2/mcp/servers?action_count=true" request, causing the command to execute.

Achieve code execution.

"Any authenticated Langflow user (including non-admin accounts) can execute arbitrary OS commands on the server with the privileges of the Langflow process," Langflow warned.

The operator installed Pawns.app, a legitimate bandwidth-sharing application that lets users earn money by sharing their internet connections, on devices without the owners’ consent.

Pawns.app account holders are rewarded for allowing traffic from other users to flow through their network, provided it runs on trusted, non-blocking IP addresses.

Even legitimate proxy networks can route suspicious traffic through volunteer-operated nodes due to insufficient oversight, potentially resulting in IP address blocks for participating users or exposing them to allegations of involvement in illegal activities.

AUR is a community-maintained, widely-used package index for Arch Linux and derivative distributions that hosts package build scripts (PKGBUILDs) for third-party and proprietary tools, beta, or older package versions that are no longer available via the official Linux distribution channels.

baslik: Is AI pentesting as good as a human pentester?
govde:
With the rise of AI pentesting, a lot of people are wondering if it’s as good as a human. Having started as a pentester twelve years ago, and having moved through similar roles to working on Intruder’s AI pentester,

I've come to understand the advantages and disadvantages of both. Here’s how they compare.

The strict methodology was never the good bit

You may expect AI pentesters to follow strict methodologies in the way that many human pentests do.

At Intruder, we experimented with this approach early on - structured systems where each agent had a specific vulnerability type to look for. What we found was that agents would miss things outside their remit entirely, or miscategorize what they did find as the one thing they'd been told to look for, causing confusing reports.

A complete lack of structure also failed to produce good results, as completely free agents without any guidance couldn’t break down and manage large applications properly. They could find interesting things, but at the cost of missing a load of other vulnerabilities in our targets.

We’ve put a lot of testing into finding the balance between these approaches, and settled on giving agents freedom with broadly defined roles to help them approach and manage large applications, and stricter guardrails to stop them causing damage.

This does mean that our AI pentester doesn’t tick off the parts of a methodology document that you’d typically see in a human pentest. That may make some people uncomfortable - a strict methodology gives people assurance that someone has gone through your application and tested everything on the list. An unauthenticated SQL injection needs to be found, and a checklist is there to make sure it does.

The methodology gives a lot of people the idea that a human pentest is a perfectly repeatable product, as any tester will be able to follow the methodology, and everything important will get found. The reality is a lot more nuanced than that though, as pentesting is a skille

If either condition doesn’t apply, the attack path doesn’t exist.

baslik: Small Agents, Smaller Blast Radius: Controlling What AI Can Do, (Fri, Oct 16th)
govde:
Small Agents, Smaller Blast Radius: Controlling What AI Can Do

I believe the cybersecurity industry may be approaching AI security the wrong way.

AI agents are becoming more powerful every day. Systems like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok can write and execute code, use command shells, browse the web, call APIs, interact with MCP servers, and access enterprise data. Yet much of the industry is taking these extraordinarily powerful, general-purpose agents and trying to make them safe by building cages around them. We add containers, policy layers, monitoring, guardrails, and humans in the loop.

I think that’s backwards. If the companies building these models struggle to control their behavior, why do we assume we can reliably contain them? And when in human history has requiring a user to click a button before something dangerous happened EVER worked?

Even if you build the perfect cage, the model you tested in your cage will eventually change. Providers retire models, and moving to a replacement means revisiting your assumptions and testing. Your application code may be unchanged, but the component deciding what to do next is different.

In my opinion, we should use these agents, which are very good at coding, to build smaller, single-purpose agents. If an agent only needs to read logs from one directory, why give it functions that can read, write, or execute things anywhere on the system?

This isn’t a new idea. It’s the principle of least privilege and seperation of duties. But somehow, when we build agents, we seem willing to hand over broad access and ask the model to use good judgment.

This is the guiding philosophy behind SANS SEC573: AI-Powered Security Automation, where we learn to vibe code these focused agents into existence. Use the powerful coding agent to build a better agent. Give the resulting agent only the access it needs to do its job.

baslik: Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks
govde:
Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks

Since mid-2025, the Kremlin has intensified restrictions on digital communications and infrastructure, very likely to suppress the organization of domestic political dissent and conduct digital surveillance within Russia. Increasingly strict measures targeting virtual private networks (VPNs), state-managed internet shutdowns, limitations on civilian communications platforms, and monitoring of domestic and foreign entities very likely represent an escalation from the approaches to censorship and surveillance pursued prior to 2024.

However, despite intensifying internet restrictions, technical and political limitations will likely prevent the Kremlin from achieving its long-held objective of a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term. The most likely scenario is that Moscow exerts extensive censorship and monitoring of online activity with increasingly strict –– though not absolute –– controls on circumvention and anonymizing tools.

Insikt Group assesses that the Kremlin’s primary objectives regarding internet restrictions are twofold: facilitating extensive surveillance of online activity to support control over the domestic information space while maintaining connectivity to the global internet, and developing national internet infrastructure under Kremlin control, enabling isolation from the global internet if the Kremlin so chooses. Efforts in support of these objectives have almost certainly provided the Kremlin with enhanced ability to control and monitor domestic online discourse.

In this environment, individuals and organizations operating in Russia are subject to increasing operational risks, including surveillance and exposure of sensitive data, challenges in conducting emergency communications, disruptions to corporate tools and digital applications, and legal risks. Proofpoint agreed Thursday to acquire Varonis Systems in a cash transaction valued at approximately $6.3 billion, combining two companies that have positioned themselves around a shared bet: that securing data has become the central problem of the AI era.

Sumit Dhawan, Proofpoint’s CEO, wrote in a blog post Wednesday that AI is changing the security equation on two fronts. Outside the enterprise, attackers are using AI to launch faster and more advanced campaigns aimed at data and critical systems. Inside, companies are deploying AI agents that have wide-ranging access to sensitive information, creating new categories of insider risk.

“Data Security — protecting data from compromise, loss, and misuse by people or AI agents — has become the defining priority for organizations seeking to realize AI’s full potential,” Dhawan wrote.

The companies frame the deal as a response to that dual pressure. In a joint announcement, they said the combined organization would serve millions of organizations globally, and described plans for helping organizations adopt and secure AI.

Proofpoint’s global reach, he wrote, includes 3.4 million customers, 2.37 trillion emails scanned annually, 410 billion data security events ingested, and more than 13,000 sensors across 105 countries. Those signals feed what the company calls its Knowledge Graph, which strengthens its AI models with intelligence on threats, human behavior and data risk. baslik: The next election influence campaign will target your AI chatbot
govde:
The next election influence campaign will target your AI chatbot

Election influence campaigns, particularly ones playing out over social media, are a dime a dozen.

Such campaigns – sometimes devised by foreign powers, other times by domestic groups – are often designed to influence the U.S. electorate. Fake accounts and online personas are created, networks of propaganda are disseminated and the campaign seeks to nudge American voters into thinking a certain way.

Mostly, these efforts are known for getting little to no traction with U.S. audiences. But while social media influence campaigns may not be effective, bad actors continue to adapt their coordinated propaganda goals to new tactics and technologies.

Enter AI chatbots, which have become a source of information and truth for many, who consult the tool for feedback and advice on everything from their careers, to their relationships with their family, as well as their politics.

But new research from VisionHeight, an Israeli threat intelligence firm, highlights how AI systems can often serve as more useful marks for influence actors than humans. To wit: someone is setting up networks of hyperlocal websites across at least 14 different states, filled with content meant to influence U.S. races.

These networks include websites with names like “Wolverine State Report” or “Peach State Bulletin.” Each state network usually has between five to six separate sites,  some presenting themselves as hard news outlets and others as opinion or editorial sites. The outlets also cite one another, creating a circular network of local credibility.

But the content on these websites does not resemble journalism, or any writing that a human would find coherent or compelling. Rather, they often include text of statements about specific candidates running in local races, directly stating they are the better candidate for a political issue.

baslik: Spyware vendors found a way to make targeted ads even worse
govde: The online advertising industry has found a new way to make itself even more unpopular, with one adtech outfit accused of helping spyware vendors infect people's phones without them even clicking an ad. Researchers at Citizen Lab say they've uncovered the first publicly confirmed case of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack being delivered through targeted online ads, with devices at Al Jazeera among those infected. The technique, dubbed "AdFection," turns advertising networks into a spyware delivery system. Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.

A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.

Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.
